title: Internet of Things (IoT) Fundamentals
topicSummary: IoT architecture, protocols (MQTT/HTTP), sensors, actuators, microcontrollers, firmware, cloud integration, case studies.

content.text: This module introduces IoT (Internet of Things) as the data acquisition layer in Urban Informatics.

items: Understand how real-world data is collected
Learn communication between devices and cloud

content.text: Definition: IoT refers to a network of physical devices that sense the environment, communicate data, and act automatically.

📖 Reading Note: The global IoT device count exceeded 15 billion in 2024 and is projected to reach 30 billion by 2030 (Statista). In smart cities, this means hundreds of thousands of devices per city — each generating data streams. India's Smart Cities Mission has already deployed over 8 lakh IoT devices across 100 cities as of 2024. A single smart streetlight does 4 things simultaneously: monitors its own health (predictive maintenance), dims when no pedestrian is nearby (energy saving), logs air quality (pollution monitoring), and counts pedestrians (urban mobility data). This multi-functionality is why IoT is the backbone of urban data collection.
Definition: IoT architecture defines how components interact from device to cloud.
Data Flow: Sensor → Microcontroller → Network → Cloud → Dashboard

📖 Reading Note: 'Edge computing' is a critical refinement of the standard IoT architecture. Instead of sending all raw sensor data to the cloud (which is bandwidth-intensive), edge computing means the microcontroller does some processing locally — e.g., averaging 60 seconds of temperature readings and sending just one number per minute instead of 60 raw readings. This reduces data transmission by 98%. In urban contexts, traffic cameras with embedded AI chips (like NVIDIA Jetson Nano) perform vehicle detection on-device and only transmit vehicle count numbers — not the actual video footage, protecting privacy and saving bandwidth.

items: Features: Lightweight, Publish/Subscribe model, Efficient for low bandwidth

content.text: 📖 Reading Note: MQTT's Publish/Subscribe model elegantly solves the IoT many-to-many communication problem. Imagine 500 pollution sensors across Mumbai, each publishing to the topic 'mumbai/pollution/PM2.5'. The MCGM (Mumbai Corporation) air quality dashboard subscribes to this topic and receives all 500 sensors' data without polling each one individually. MQTT runs over TCP/IP and uses only 2 bytes of protocol overhead per message (vs. hundreds for HTTP headers). Tools like Mosquitto (open-source MQTT broker) and HiveMQ are used in actual smart city deployments — free to experiment with at test.mosquitto.org.
Definition: Sensors are devices that collect data from the environment.

📖 Reading Note: Sensor selection involves a cost-accuracy trade-off. For urban air quality monitoring: Electrochemical sensors (₹200-500 per unit) measure NO2 and O3 with ±20% accuracy — suitable for dense neighborhood networks. Optical particle counters (₹5,000-15,000) measure PM2.5 with ±5% accuracy — suitable for reference stations. India's Pollution Control Boards deploy both: a few high-accuracy reference stations and a dense network of lower-cost sensors for spatial coverage. The combination gives both precise calibration points and citywide spatial resolution — a data fusion approach called 'sparse + dense' monitoring.
Definition: Actuators perform actions based on data received from sensors/controllers.

📖 Reading Note: The sensor-actuator feedback loop is the core of closed-loop urban control systems. Example: In Surat's flood management system — a water level sensor (sensor) in the Tapi River detects a rising water level → sends data via MQTT to cloud → ML model predicts flood threshold will be crossed in 2 hours → cloud sends command signal → motorized flood gates (actuators) at storm drains partially close → city sends automated emergency alerts to registered citizens. The entire loop from sensor reading to actuator response takes < 3 minutes. This is urban informatics at its most impactful.
Definition: Microcontrollers are small computing devices that control sensors and actuators.

📖 Reading Note: Key differences matter in hardware selection: Arduino Uno (ATmega328P) — no WiFi, simple digital/analog I/O, 32KB flash, best for simple sensor reading + serial output. ESP8266/ESP32 — built-in WiFi, 4MB flash, great for direct MQTT cloud publishing, used in most production urban IoT nodes. Raspberry Pi 4 — full Linux computer (1.8GHz, 4GB RAM), runs Python/TensorFlow/OpenCV, used for edge AI (vehicle detection at intersections) but costs 10x more than ESP32. For a budget urban air quality network of 100 nodes, ESP32 (~₹250 each) beats Raspberry Pi (~₹4,000 each) on cost efficiency.
Definition: Firmware is the software embedded in hardware devices that controls sensors, handles communication, and executes device logic.
Example: Code running on Arduino to read temperature and send data to the cloud.
Definition: Connecting IoT devices to cloud platforms for storage, processing, and visualization.

📖 Reading Note: ThingSpeak (by MathWorks) and Blynk are free IoT cloud platforms that are ideal for learning and prototyping. ThingSpeak lets you send sensor data from an ESP8266 via a single HTTP GET request, then visualizes it on auto-refreshing charts. An urban student project could use ThingSpeak to build a real PM2.5 monitoring dashboard for your college campus in one weekend — sensor (MQ135 gas sensor + Arduino) + ESP8266 + ThingSpeak free account. ThingSpeak also supports MATLAB analytics for trend detection. These platforms lower the barrier to real-world urban data collection.

items: Smart Traffic System: Sensors detect vehicles → Microcontroller processes → Cloud optimizes signals.
Air Quality Monitoring: Gas sensors measure pollution → Data sent to cloud → Dashboard displays AQI.
Smart Parking: Ultrasonic sensors detect availability → Mobile app shows free slots.
Smart Street Lighting: Motion sensors detect presence → Lights turn on/off automatically.

content.text: How Week 10 Concepts Connect Across the Course:

rows: IoT architecture IS the detailed engineering breakdown of 'digital infrastructure' introduced conceptually in Week 1
MQTT streams event data in real-time to brokers; Apache Kafka (Week 12) scales this pattern to handle city-wide sensor event floods
Each sensor type maps to a data type from Week 2: temperature sensor → structured numerical data; camera → unstructured image data; GPS → geospatial data
An actuator's decision (open gate / turn on light / stop traffic) is a real-world classification output — the ML model classifies a situation, the actuator acts on it
Week 11 is the hands-on implementation of the microcontroller concepts introduced here — ideally studied immediately after Week 10
The cloud platforms (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud) introduced in Week 3 for data storage are the same platforms IoT devices in Week 10 send data to — completing the pipeline

content.text: 🔗 Big Picture: Week 10 is the 'physical-digital bridge' of the course. Data doesn't start in a database — it starts in the real physical world (traffic, temperature, air quality). Week 10 explains how the physical world becomes digital data. Without this layer, Weeks 2–9's data analysis has no data to work with. IoT is the source; everything else is downstream.

examSummary: IoT = connected devices collecting and acting on data
MQTT = Publish/Subscribe (lightweight for IoT); HTTP = Request/Response (web)
Sensors → data collection; Actuators → action execution
Firmware = embedded software running on devices
keyInsight: Week 10 connects the physical world to digital systems. 👉 If Week 9 = 'Advanced intelligence', Week 10 = 'Real-world data collection and automation'.
